justice: The street cross-section appears to prioritize a single shared vehicle space with no dedicated sidewalk, limiting equitable space allocation for pedestrians and cyclists.

A utility pole stands within the main travel corridor, creating a physical bottleneck that disproportionately affects users needing more space (e.g., people walking side-by-side, pushing strollers, or carrying goods).
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked pedestrian-priority space; the uneven edge along the left wall suggests barriers for barrier-free movement.
safety: No lane markings, crosswalks, or visible traffic-calming devices on the narrow roadway; shared-space ambiguity increases pedestrian–vehicle conflict risk.
A parked car encroaches on the narrow street, reducing sightlines and forcing all users to weave around it in the same corridor.

Multiple overhead wires and closely spaced poles create visual clutter and potential maintenance hazards; the pole near the center of the roadway is a direct collision risk for drivers/cyclists at night or in low visibility.
livability: Residential buildings and boundary walls line the street, but the frontage is mostly closed (long wall on the left), offering limited active edges that typically support everyday street life.
There is some greenery (shrubs/planting bed on the right and trees in the distance), which can support a calmer neighborhood feel.
Lack of visible benches, small public nodes, or shopfronts suggests limited opportunities for resting and social interaction along the segment.
sustainability: Some planting and shrub beds on the right provide minor green infrastructure and potential micro-habitat, though coverage is limited along the full length.
Car presence and lack of dedicated active-transport facilities indicate the street design does not strongly incentivize low-carbon mode shift.
No visible stormwater features (e.g., permeable paving, bioswale inlets) and extensive hard paving suggest limited support for rainwater infiltration.
aesthetics: The right-side planting strip with mixed shrubs adds color and softens the street edge, improving visual quality compared with fully hardscaped edges.
The left side is dominated by a long tiled wall with posted notices, creating a monotonous and less inviting streetscape.
Overhead utility wires form a dense web across the sky, reducing visual neatness and perceived order.
comfort: Limited street tree canopy over the roadway means low shade provision; thermal comfort may be poor during hot/sunny periods despite some greenery at the edges.
Physical comfort is reduced by uneven edges and the narrow shared corridor, where pedestrians must negotiate with vehicles and parked cars rather than walk in a protected space.
Psychological comfort is weakened by the close proximity of vehicles in a constrained lane and by the obstructing pole in the travel path, which can increase perceived stress for all users.
walkability: No clearly delineated sidewalk; pedestrians appear to share the same paved surface as vehicles, reducing perceived and actual walking safety.
Obstructions (parked car and a pole within/adjacent to the travel line) interrupt continuous, predictable pedestrian movement.
The street is relatively narrow and seems low-speed by geometry, which can help walking comfort, but the lack of separation and markings still constrains walkability.
bikeability: No bike lane markings or physical protection; cyclists must mix with vehicles on a narrow corridor, increasing overtaking and squeeze risks.
A parked car narrows the usable width, creating door-zone/avoidance maneuvers and forcing cyclists toward the center of the lane.
The central/near-lane utility pole and irregular edge conditions create fixed-object hazards and reduce safe operating space for cycling.
